<!-- FOOTER: shared author names and university logos. -->
{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

<!-- NOTES: presenter guidance and reading-view explanations. -->

::: {.notes}
Source: [Tutorial §2 and §4](assets/tutorial.pdf)

Read each row from left to right: name the term, give its meaning, then connect it to the inventory problem.
State is visible on arrival; advance to reveal action, uncertainty, transition, cost, and policy one at a
time. Finally reveal the Markov decision process definition. Here t indexes periods. The numerical example
fixes one possible first period: stock 0, order 2, demand 5, then inventory −3 (three units of unmet demand);
it need not match the audience's random draw on slide 3. G_t is random demand and g_t is its observed
realization. Inventory can be negative to represent unmet demand. The opening animation carries all unmet
demand forward. The later full transition clips the result to the model's backlog and storage limits; keep
that detail for the later inventory slide and technical backup. With independent demand and immediate
replenishment, current inventory together with the period index is sufficient; lead times would require
outstanding orders in the state. c(s,a) averages immediate costs over demand, while the animation displays
realized costs. The illustrative policy is π(s) = min{6, max{0, 6−s}}, so stock 0 gives order 6 and stock 1
gives order 5. It is a rule for all states, not one particular order or a claim of optimality.
:::

## Bellman’s equation and the policy objective {#b-bellman-objective .content-slide .bellman-slide}

<!-- SLIDE CONTENT -->

::: {.slide-body}
```{=html}
<p class="bellman-definition">
  <span class="bellman-value"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math></span>
  is the minimum expected cost from period <i>t</i> onward, starting in state <i>s</i>.
</p>
```

::: {.bellman-equation-native .fragment data-fragment-index="0"}
$$
\underbrace{V_t^*(s)}_{\text{optimal cost}}=\underbrace{\min_{a\in \mathcal{A}(s)}}_{\text{feasible action}}\left\{\underbrace{c_t(s,a)}_{\text{cost now}}+\underbrace{\mathbb E[V_{t+1}^*(s')\mid s,a]}_{\text{future cost}}\right\}
$$
:::

```{=html}
<div class="bellman-recursion-tail">
  <p class="bellman-boundary">
    <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>s′</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>·</mo><mo>|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>
    &nbsp;·&nbsp;
    <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>…</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></math> &nbsp;·&nbsp;
    <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>T</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>:
    no additional terminal cost.
  </p>
</div>
<div class="bellman-connection fragment" data-fragment-index="5">
  <h3>
    Connection to the MDP formulation
  </h3>
  <div class="bellman-objective-link">
    <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" displaystyle="true" aria-label="The minimum expected total cost over all feasible policies equals V star at period zero and the initial state."><munder><mo>min</mo><mi>π</mi></munder><mspace width="0.3em"/><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">E</mi><mi>π</mi></msup><mo>[</mo><mrow><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo>]</mo><mo>=</mo><mrow mathcolor="#267f77"><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>
  </div>
  <p>
    The optimal objective is the value at the <strong>initial period and state</strong>. For our inventory
    example, <i>s</i><sub>0</sub> = 0, so it is <span class="bellman-value"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mn>0</mn><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math></span>.
  </p>
  <p class="bellman-profit-note">
    For a profit-maximization formulation, define <i>V</i> using profits and a maximum; the initial value is
    then the optimal expected profit.
  </p>
</div>
```
:::

<!-- FOOTER: shared author names and university logos. -->
{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

<!-- NOTES: presenter guidance and reading-view explanations. -->

::: {.notes}
Source: [Tutorial §2.1, Bellman optimality equations](assets/tutorial.pdf). Cost-minimization convention
matches the opening inventory example.

Define V_t^* as the minimum expected remaining cost. Reveal the equation, then reveal its four underbraces and
matching labels individually from left to right: optimal remaining cost, feasible action choice, expected
immediate cost, and expected optimal continuation cost. c_t already averages realized period costs; those
costs are not counted twice. P_t is the transition distribution from the MDP formulation slide. The horizon is finite and
undiscounted, and V_T^* = 0 means no additional terminal cost; final-period holding and stockout costs remain
in c_{T−1}.

The last reveal connects Bellman’s equation directly to the policy optimization objective, with each
period cost written as c_t(s_t, π_t(s_t)). The Bellman recursion itself minimizes over a feasible current
action a. For a fixed initial state s_0, the minimum over feasible policies of the expected sum of costs is
exactly V_0^*(s_0). The subscript 0 is the initial period; the argument s_0 is the initial state. Starting the
inventory example with zero stock therefore gives V_0^*(0). This is an optimal expected total, not the
realized cost of one animation run. Keep the displayed formula in costs to match the inventory formulation. If the model instead
maximizes profits, its value function is defined using profits and max, and its initial value is the optimal
expected profit. For the specific reward transformation r_t = −c_t, the optimal reward value is the negative
of the cost value; do not equate profit to the displayed minimum-cost value. Do not add a backward-induction
walkthrough here.
:::

```{=html}
      <ul class="method-references">
        <li>
          <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470316887" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="puterman_markov_2014"><strong>Puterman</strong><span>Markov
          Decision Processes: Discrete Stochastic Dynamic Programming</span></a>
        </li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="method-detail" role="region" id="method-panel-value" aria-labelledby="method-button-value">
      <h3>
        Value-function approximation
      </h3>
      <p class="method-description">
        Replace a value table with a function whose parameters are fitted using simulated transitions or
        model-based updates. Choose actions using estimated future value.
      </p>
      <p class="method-limit">
        <strong>Consideration.</strong> Performance depends on the representation and where the method samples
        or evaluates states.
      </p>
      <h4>
        Selected references
      </h4>
      <ul class="method-references">
        <li>
          <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118029176" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="Powell2011"><strong>Powell
          (2011)</strong><span>Approximate Dynamic Programming: Solving the Curses of Dimensionality</span></a>
        </li>
        <li>
          <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/educ.1063.0027" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="powell2006"><strong>Powell
          &amp; Topaloglu (2006)</strong><span>Approximate Dynamic Programming for Large-Scale Resource
          Allocation Problems</span></a>
        </li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="method-detail" role="region" id="method-panel-policy" aria-labelledby="method-button-policy">
      <h3>
        Policy search &amp; learning
      </h3>
      <p class="method-description">
        Parameterize the policy and improve it using sampled trajectories. Policy-gradient and actor–critic
        methods are examples within reinforcement learning.
      </p>
      <p class="method-limit">
        <strong>Consideration.</strong> Exploration, training stability, and enforcing constraints require
        design choices.
      </p>
      <h4>
        Selected references
      </h4>
      <ul class="method-references">
        <li>
          <a href="https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262039246/reinforcement-learning/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="SuttonBarto2018"><strong>Sutton
          &amp; Barto (2018)</strong><span>Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction</span></a>
        </li>
        <li>
          <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118029176" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="Powell2011"><strong>Powell
          (2011)</strong><span>Approximate Dynamic Programming: Solving the Curses of Dimensionality</span></a>
        </li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="method-detail" role="region" id="method-panel-tree" aria-labelledby="method-button-tree">
      <h3>
        Simulation &amp; tree search
      </h3>
      <p class="method-description">
        Simulate possible future decisions and outcomes. Monte Carlo tree search focuses simulations on
        promising branches, then selects the next action.
      </p>
      <p class="method-limit">
        <strong>Consideration.</strong> Requires a simulator; the branching factor and planning depth affect
        the computation needed.
      </p>
      <h4>
        Selected references
      </h4>
      <ul class="method-references">
        <li>
          <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/educ.2017.0166" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="fu2017"><strong>Fu
          (2017)</strong><span>Markov Decision Processes, AlphaGo, and Monte Carlo Tree Search: Back to the Future</span></a>
        </li>
        <li>
          <a href="https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262039246/reinforcement-learning/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="SuttonBarto2018"><strong>Sutton
          &amp; Barto (2018)</strong><span>Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction</span></a>
        </li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div
      class="method-detail"
      role="region"
      id="method-panel-optimization"
      aria-labelledby="method-button-optimization"
    >
      <h3>
        Optimization-based approximations
      </h3>
      <p class="method-description">
        Fit approximate values through linear programs, or relax shared constraints to separate component
        problems. These models can also provide bounds under appropriate conditions.
      </p>
      <p class="method-limit">
        <strong>Consideration.</strong> Choosing features, finding violated constraints, and recovering
        feasible policies can be difficult.
      </p>
      <h4>
        Selected references
      </h4>
      <ul class="method-references">
        <li>
          <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.51.6.850.24925" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="de_farias_linear_2003"><strong>de
          Farias &amp; Van Roy (2003)</strong><span>The Linear Programming Approach to Approximate Dynamic Programming</span></a>
        </li>
        <li>
          <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.1070.0445" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="adelman2008"><strong>Adelman
          &amp; Mersereau (2008)</strong><span>Relaxations of Weakly Coupled Stochastic Dynamic Programs</span></a>
        </li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="method-detail" role="region" id="method-panel-structure" aria-labelledby="method-button-structure">
      <h3>
        Index &amp; fluid policies
      </h3>
      <p class="method-description">
        Index policies rank alternatives using a priority score. Fluid approximations replace random
        population flows with deterministic quantities and derive decisions from that model.
      </p>
      <p class="method-limit">
        <strong>Consideration.</strong> Guarantees depend on structural assumptions or limiting regimes; these
        are not general-purpose exact methods.
      </p>
      <h4>
        Selected references
      </h4>
      <ul class="method-references">
        <li>
          <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10872" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="scully2025"><strong>Scully
          &amp; Terenin (2025)</strong><span>The Gittins Index: A Design Principle for Decision-Making Under Uncertainty</span></a>
        </li>
        <li>
          <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.2016.1531" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" data-citation="bertsimas2016decomposable"><strong>Bertsimas
          &amp; Mišić (2016)</strong><span>Decomposable Markov Decision Processes: A Fluid Optimization Approach</span></a>
        </li>
      </ul>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="methods-overlap">
  These families overlap: learning, search, and optimization can be combined.
</p>
```
:::

and approximate linear programming is also value-function approximation. Separate the optimization family here

<!-- NOTES: presenter guidance and reading-view explanations. -->

::: {.notes}
Source: [Tutorial introduction, modeling-to-solution gap and mathematical-programming analogy](assets/tutorial.pdf).

Solver logo sources:
[Gurobi logo on the official SCIP site](https://scipopt.org/images/GurobiLogo_Black-1-1-1.svg),
[Hexaly](https://www.hexaly.com/wp-content/themes/hexaly/assets/images/hexaly-logo-orange.svg), and
[SCIP](https://scipopt.org/images/newscippy.png). These are examples of solvers, not a claim about identical
capabilities. The result illustration corresponds to the displayed mathematical program: x₁ = 0, x₂ = 5 gives
objective 10. Since 3x₁ + 2x₂ = 2(x₁ + x₂) + x₁ ≥ 10 for every feasible solution, it is optimal with zero gap.
This is an illustrative result, not a live solver run.

Transition from the learning outcomes: we want to reduce the work of choosing an approximation and configuring
its solution method, while retaining the model features that matter for decisions. This tutorial focuses on
approximations built with mathematical optimization. Start with the question at the top, then explain why
mathematical optimization is our inspiration. The broader method survey is available in technical backup.

The workflow is to model a problem, solve it, and use the solution to refine the formulation. Evaluate the
solution and its quality, then add cuts or revise the model when useful. In mixed-integer programming, the
user specifies variables, an objective, and constraints; the solver manages much of the search and reports
feasible solutions and bounds when available. The small program illustrates the output available for
evaluation; its exact optimum does not itself require further refinement. This does not imply that all
formulations are easy or that all runs find an optimum. This introductory analogy groups formulation
improvements broadly; the next slide distinguishes refinement across solves from solver operations such as cut
generation within a solve.

Return to the lower question: how can we offer a comparable modeling and solution workflow for MDPs, where the
output is a policy? We need representations and approximation methods that do more of the work currently left
to the user. This motivates the next slide's construct–optimize–refine framework. The analogy is an aspiration
for accessibility and useful performance, not a promise that arbitrary MDPs become easy to solve. The opening
question is visible on arrival. Advance to reveal the context, inspiration, Model, Solve, Refine, and closing
question in that order. Each arrow appears with its destination. The model illustration is an illustrative
two-variable linear program; “s.t.” means “subject to.” There are no numerical controls or automatic animations.
:::

<!-- NOTES: presenter guidance and reading-view explanations. -->

::: {.notes}
Source: [Tutorial introduction and §2.3](assets/tutorial.pdf)

The definition is visible on arrival. Explain that the method automates approximation choices using information
about the problem instance or the solution process. The aim is less manual design effort together with useful
performance. Adaptation can occur in one or more stages; it need not occur in all three. In the later delayed
allocation example, the current LP solution guides which feasible assortments to represent next. This is an
example of adaptation during refinement, not the definition of all self adapting approximations.

COR stands for construct–optimize–refine. Construction chooses the approximation and model. Optimization fits
its parameters. Refinement changes the representation across solves. Adaptation inside a fixed-model solve
belongs to optimize. A self-adapting method need not use a separate refine stage. The aim is accessibility
together with useful performance, rather than automation alone.

Use six advances to walk through the diagram: reveal the representation and model; connect to optimize; reveal
the fitted parameters; connect to refine; reveal the quality assessment; then close the feedback loop. All
earlier elements remain visible. Within Construct, a complicated piecewise cost function appears first, then
an initial smooth representation is drawn. Optimize begins with that same smooth curve already complete; after
a short pause, its parameters change continuously to fit the fixed piecewise function more closely. The
reference stays identical across all three sketches, and Refine shows the final fitted curve with a region to
inspect. This is a schematic illustration of representation and fitting, not a live optimizer, computed MDP
solution, or error certificate. The known reference function is a teaching device; actual MDP approximation
methods need not know the true value function and solve the appropriate constrained models. The fitted
approximation can be used to select actions. A bound or simulated policy cost can guide refinement without
necessarily identifying a particular state region. Enrichment may add features, strengthen a formulation, or
change which states receive emphasis. The final arrow represents changes across solves, not iterations of the
solver. The reading view and reduced-motion mode show the final fitted curve without animation.
:::

The initial collection in both periods is empty, backpack+cooler, and tent only. Feature nothing is a valid
reference action. Backpack+tent is also feasible (2+6=8), but omitted initially. The tuple is a complete
display assignment with one binary position for each named product. The collection is not a policy: it lists
which actions are represented. State-independent feasibility does not imply state-independent rewards or
policies. Construct includes both selecting this initial collection and building the uncertainty model on the
following slides.

## The display problem as an MDP {#b-display-mdp .content-slide .assortment-slide}

<!-- SLIDE CONTENT -->

::: {.slide-body}
<div class="assort-definitions">
 <div>
  <b>State s = (s<sub>B</sub>, s<sub>C</sub>, s<sub>T</sub>)</b><span>Demand information for each
  product:<br>unknown, known low, or known high</span>
 </div>
 <div>
  <b>Action a = (a<sub>B</sub>, a<sub>C</sub>, a<sub>T</sub>)</b><span>Feature (1) or do not feature
  (0)<br>Order: backpack, cooler, tent</span>
 </div>
 <div>
  <b>Reward r<sub>t,j</sub>(s<sub>j</sub>, a<sub>j</sub>)</b><span>Expected incremental profit<br>from product
  j in period t</span>
 </div>
</div>

::: {.assort-bellman .fragment data-fragment-index="0"}
$$
V_t(s)=\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\left\{\underbrace{\sum_{j=1}^{J}r_{t,j}(s_j,a_j)}_{\text{current profit}}+\underbrace{\mathbb E[V_{t+1}(s')\mid s,a]}_{\text{future profit}}\right\}
$$
:::

<div class="assort-equation-key fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
 <div>
  <strong>Feasible assortments</strong><span>2a<sub>B</sub> + 3a<sub>C</sub> + 6a<sub>T</sub> ≤ 8<br>Each
  a<sub>j</sub> is 0 or 1.</span>
 </div>
 <div>
  <strong>Local transitions</strong><span>s′<sub>j</sub> ∼ P<sub>t,j</sub>(· | s<sub>j</sub>,
  a<sub>j</sub>)<br>Observe sales; update demand information.</span>
 </div>
 <div>
  <strong>Optimal total profit</strong><span>V₀(s₀), with V₂(s) = 0<br>Two periods; no terminal reward.</span>
 </div>
</div>
<p class="assort-takeaway assort-weak-coupling fragment" data-fragment-index="2">
 <strong>Weakly coupled:</strong> separate product rewards and transitions, linked by the display-space budget.
</p>
:::

<!-- NOTES: presenter guidance and reading-view explanations. -->

::: {.notes}
Source: tutorial section 3, weakly coupled MDP formulation.

Introduce the tuple order explicitly: (backpack, cooler, tent). For example, (1,0,0) means feature only the
backpack. These are binary decisions, not order quantities or probabilities. J=3 here. The state records
demand information, so a product's expected reward changes as its demand type becomes known. The Bellman
policy can depend on all observed states even though the feasible action set does not. The expectation uses
the product of the local transition probabilities. V_0(s_0) is optimal expected total profit. The display
example maximizes profit; the earlier inventory example minimizes cost.
:::

## Linear programming model {#s25 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide .exact-lp-slide}

::: {.slide-body}

<div class="equation-box compact-equation optimality-equation" style="border-left:3px solid var(--teal)">
<h3><strong>Bellman optimality equation</strong></h3>

$$
V^*(s)=\min_{a\in\mathcal{A}(s)}\left\{c(s,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{S}}V^*(s')\,P(ds'\mid s,a)\right\},\qquad s\in\mathcal{S}.
$$

</div>

<div class="lp-model-stage">

<div class="equation-box compact-equation lp-model-equation fragment" data-fragment-index="0" style="border-left:3px solid var(--accent)">
<h3><strong>Exact linear program</strong></h3>

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_{V:\,\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb R}\quad
&\int_{\mathcal{S}}V(s)\,\nu(ds)\\
\text{s.t.}\quad
&V(s)\le c(s,a)+\gamma\int_{\mathcal{S}}V(s')\,P(ds'\mid s,a),
\qquad \forall s\in\mathcal{S},\ a\in\mathcal{A}(s).
\end{aligned}
$$


</div>

```{=html}
<div class="lp-value-plot" aria-label="Conceptual animation of Bellman-feasible value functions rising to the optimal value function">
 <div class="lp-value-chart">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 620 280" role="img" aria-label="Value versus state. Feasible curves rise from below toward V star.">
   <defs><clipPath id="lp-value-clip"><rect x="50" y="28" width="540" height="202"/></clipPath><marker id="lp-value-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10Z" fill="#a4592f"/></marker></defs>
   <g clip-path="url(#lp-value-clip)"><path data-value-shade fill="#e6eef7"/><g data-value-guides fill="none" stroke="#a8b4bd" stroke-width="2"/><path data-value-moving fill="none" stroke="#267f77" stroke-width="3.5"/><path data-value-optimum fill="none" stroke="#183c84" stroke-width="4"/><path data-value-push fill="none" stroke="#a4592f" stroke-width="2.5" marker-end="url(#lp-value-arrow)"/></g>
   <path d="M50 28V230H590" fill="none" stroke="#5f7180" stroke-width="1.2"/>
   <g fill="#5f7180" font-family="Avenir Next,Segoe UI,sans-serif" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle"><text x="50" y="250">−4</text><text x="185" y="250">0</text><text x="320" y="250">4</text><text x="455" y="250">8</text><text x="590" y="250">12</text><text x="320" y="274">state s</text><text transform="translate(18 132) rotate(-90)">value</text></g>
   <g font-size="15" font-family="Georgia,serif"><path d="M65 17H100" stroke="#a8b4bd" stroke-width="2"/><text x="108" y="22" fill="#5f7180">feasible V</text><path d="M340 17H375" stroke="#183c84" stroke-width="4"/><text x="383" y="22" fill="#183c84">V*</text></g>
  </svg>
 </div>
 <div class="lp-value-explanation">
```
<p class="lp-value-heading">Maximizing the objective pushes feasible values upward</p>

$$
\max_V\int_{\mathcal{S}}V(s)\,\nu(ds)
$$

```{=html}
 <button type="button" class="lp-value-replay">Replay animation</button>
 </div>
</div>
<span class="fragment lp-plot-step" data-fragment-index="1" aria-hidden="true"></span>
```

</div>

:::

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Begin with the discounted-cost Bellman optimality equation. Advance once to reveal its equivalent exact linear program. The decision variable in the LP is the full value function; the objective averages it under the state-relevance distribution. Every feasible state-action pair contributes a Bellman inequality. Advance again to replace the LP with a conceptual animated plot; a further advance moves directly to the next slide. The animation uses V_delta = V* - delta, with delta decreasing to zero. Constant downward shifts of V* are Bellman-feasible in a discounted cost MDP: their Bellman slack gains (1-gamma)delta. Hence raising this family increases the integral objective and reaches V*. The plot is schematic, not a numerical inventory solution or an optimization algorithm. Being below V* is necessary but not sufficient for Bellman feasibility. Under the usual assumptions V* is the pointwise largest Bellman-feasible function and an LP optimizer. An objective under nu does not distinguish differences on nu-null sets without additional support/regularity assumptions.
:::

::: {.notes}
The exact linear program is visible on arrival. Its infinitely many constraints and full-function decision motivate the two bottlenecks. The left panel holds the value function approximation fixed: reveal construction of the saddle-point model, optimization, refinement of that model, and the return arrow in successive advances. The right panel instead refines the value function approximation: reveal construction, optimization, refinement, and the return arrow. Each feedback arrow returns to construction for another solve. These are two distinct modeling loops. The left loop does not add VFA features; the right loop changes the VFA. This conceptual formulation-refinement loop does not assert that the particular PSMD algorithm has a separate outer Refine stage.
:::

## Approximate linear program {#s27 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide}

::: {.slide-body}

<div class="badge">Theory · §4.1</div>

<h3>ALP Construction</h3>

<div class="alp-inputs">
<div class="equation-box alp-input">
<p><strong>Features or basis functions</strong></p>

$\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_N:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb R$

<p>Choose the functions used to represent value.</p>
</div>
<div class="equation-box alp-input">
<p><strong>Weights</strong></p>

$\beta:=(\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_N)\in\mathbb R^{N+1}$

<p>Optimize the coefficients of the approximation.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="equation-box compact-equation fragment" data-fragment-index="0">
<p class="center"><strong>Finite-dimensional value function approximation (VFA)</strong></p>

$$
V_\beta(s)=\beta_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\beta_n\varphi_n(s),
\qquad \beta\in\mathbb R^{N+1}
$$
</div>

<div class="equation-box compact-equation fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left:3px solid var(--accent)">
<p class="center"><strong>Semi-infinite approximate linear program (ALP)</strong></p>

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\beta\in B}\quad
    & \mathbb E_\nu[V_\beta(s)] \\
\text{s.t.}\quad
    & V_\beta(s) \le c(s,a)
      +\gamma\,\mathbb E[V_\beta(S')\mid s,a], \quad \forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}(s).
\end{aligned}
$$


</div>

:::

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Introduce the two top boxes: fixed features or basis functions on the left and optimized weights on the right. Advance to combine them into the finite-dimensional VFA, then advance to the semi-infinite ALP below it. The coefficient vector is finite, but feasibility must hold for every continuous state and every feasible action in the set $\mathcal{A}(s)$. That is the tension driving Section 4: the representation is compact, while finding the important constraints remains difficult.
:::


<!-- ====================================================================
SLIDE 28 — Constraint violation function
==================================================================== -->

## Constraint violation function {#s28 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide .cv-general-slide}

::: {.slide-body}

<div class="cv-derivation" data-cv-step="0">
<p class="cv-step-heading" data-cv-heading>
<span data-cv-heading-step="0">Start from the ALP formulation</span>
<span data-cv-heading-step="1" hidden>Substitute the VFA formulation: <span class="cv-heading-formula">$V_\beta(s)=\beta_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\beta_n\varphi_n(s)$</span></span>
<span data-cv-heading-step="2" hidden>Collect the intercept on the left</span>
<span data-cv-heading-step="3" hidden>Divide by $1-\gamma>0$ and define $f(\beta;s,a)$</span>
</p>

<div class="equation-box cv-model">
<p class="center"><strong>Semi-infinite approximate linear program (ALP)</strong></p>
$$
\max_{\beta\in B}\quad \mathbb E_\nu[V_\beta(s)]
$$
<p class="cv-subject">subject to</p>
<div class="cv-constraint-stages">
<div class="cv-constraint-stage" data-cv-stage="0">
$$
V_\beta(s)\le c(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb E[V_\beta(S')\mid s,a]
$$
</div>
<div class="cv-constraint-stage" data-cv-stage="1">
$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\beta_n\varphi_n(s)
&\le c(s,a)+\gamma\beta_0 +\gamma\sum_{n=1}^{N}\beta_n\mathbb E[\varphi_n(S')\mid s,a]
\end{aligned}
$$
</div>
<div class="cv-constraint-stage" data-cv-stage="2">
$$
(1-\gamma)\beta_0\le c(s,a)-\sum_{n=1}^{N}\beta_n\!\left(\varphi_n(s)-\gamma\,\mathbb E[\varphi_n(S')\mid s,a]\right)
$$
</div>
<div class="cv-constraint-stage" data-cv-stage="3">
$$
\beta_0\le f(\beta;s,a):=\frac{c(s,a)-\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\beta_n\!\left(\varphi_n(s)-\gamma\,\mathbb E[\varphi_n(S')\mid s,a]\right)}{1-\gamma}
$$
</div>
</div>
<p class="center cv-domain">For every feasible pair $(s,a)$.</p>
</div>
<p class="cv-violation-note">The constraint is violated when $\beta_0>f(\beta;s,a)$.</p>
<span class="fragment cv-step-1" data-fragment-index="0" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="fragment cv-step-2" data-fragment-index="1" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="fragment cv-step-3" data-fragment-index="2" aria-hidden="true"></span>
</div>

:::

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Start with the generic semi-infinite ALP, keeping its objective unchanged throughout. First advance: substitute the feature expansion for both V_beta(s) and V_beta(S'). The expectation of the constant beta-zero is beta-zero because the transition kernel is a probability measure. Second advance: move gamma beta-zero to the left and collect the remaining feature terms on the right. Third advance: divide by positive one minus gamma and name the resulting intercept threshold f(beta;s,a). Each displayed constraint replaces the previous one; no quadratic inventory specialization is used. The next advance proceeds to Inventory control example.

The function f depends on the nonintercept coefficients even though the notation retains the full beta vector. It is an upper threshold on beta-zero, rather than itself a signed Bellman residual. A pair is violated precisely when beta-zero exceeds f; the original Bellman residual is (1-gamma)(beta-zero-f). The subsequent inventory landscape applies this generic derivation to the quadratic basis.
:::

::: {.notes}
Use the left-side scale to distinguish backlog from stock and identify the state s. The marked point is illustrative. Then reveal the order arrow and demand distribution, followed by transition and expected cost on successive advances. This is a one-item, periodic-review MDP. The state is the inventory position before ordering. The action is an order placed before demand. Demand then creates raw ending inventory X; the nested maximum and minimum enforce the backlog and storage limits to produce the next state. The cost formula attaches a separate economic meaning to each hinge term. The same four colors connect the transition regions to the cost terms. Purchase cost is incurred when ordering; the other costs depend on the demand outcome. Expected cost averages over demand at a fixed state and action.
:::

## Constraint violation function: illustration {#s30 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide .violation-slide}

::: {.slide-body}

<div class="inventory-alp-inputs">
<div class="equation-box">
<p class="center"><strong>Basis functions</strong></p>

$$\varphi_1(s)=s,\qquad \varphi_2(s)=s^2.$$

</div>
<div class="equation-box">
<p class="center"><strong>Value function approximation</strong></p>

$$V_\beta(s)=\beta_0+\beta_1s+\beta_2s^2.$$

</div>
</div>
<div class="equation-box inventory-threshold">
<p class="center"><strong>Constraint violation function</strong></p>

$$
f(\beta;s,a)=\frac{c(s,a)-\beta_1\!\left(s-\gamma\mathbb E[S'\mid s,a]\right)-\beta_2\!\left(s^2-\gamma\mathbb E[(S')^2\mid s,a]\right)}{1-\gamma}.
$$

</div>

```{=html}
<div class="continuous-python-lab fragment" data-fragment-index="0" data-continuous-python data-demo-id="constraint-violation" data-demo-autorun="true">
 <label class="demo-editor-label" for="demo-constraint-violation">Edit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&#92;beta_1</annotation></semantics></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&#92;beta_2</annotation></semantics></math>, then choose Run Python</label>
 <textarea id="demo-constraint-violation" data-demo-editor rows="3" spellcheck="false" aria-label="Editable Python for Constraint violation function">beta_1 = 2.0
beta_2 = -2.0
plot_violation(beta_1, beta_2, 81, 51)</textarea>
 <div class="demo-controls">
  <button type="button" data-demo-run>Run Python</button>
  <button type="button" data-demo-stop disabled>Stop</button>

  <span data-demo-status role="status"></span>
 </div>
 <div class="demo-output" data-demo-output aria-live="polite"><p class="demo-hint">Run Python to generate the plot.</p></div>
</div>
```

:::

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Apply the preceding general derivation with phi-one(s)=s and phi-two(s)=s squared. The result shows that each pair imposes an upper threshold f on beta-zero. Darker, smaller values are more restrictive, and a point is violated when beta-zero exceeds that threshold. The orange point is only a grid minimum, not a proof of the continuous global minimum.
:::

## Regularized saddle point problem {#s31 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide}

::: {.slide-body}



<div class="equation-box compact-equation" style="border-left:3px solid var(--teal)">
<p class="center"><strong>Define the feasible domain and admissible densities first</strong></p>

$$
D:=\{(s,a):s\in\mathcal{S},\ a\in \mathcal{A}(s)\},
\qquad
Y:=\left\{y\ge0:\ y\text{ continuous on }D,\ \int_Dy(s,a)\,d(s,a)=1\right\}.
$$

<!-- <p class="tiny muted center" style="margin:0">Also write $g(\beta):=\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n\mathbb E_\nu[\varphi_n(S)]$ for the non-intercept part of the ALP objective.</p> -->
</div>

<div class="saddle-stages">
<div class="equation-box saddle-stage fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="0">
<h3>Start from the ALP</h3>

$$
\begin{aligned}\max_{\beta_0,\,\beta\in B}\quad &\beta_0+\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n\mathbb E_\nu[\varphi_n(s)]\\\mathrm{s.t.}\quad &\beta_0\le f(\beta;s,a),\qquad\forall(s,a)\in D.\end{aligned}
$$



</div>
<div class="equation-box saddle-stage fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="0">
<h3>Replace all constraints by their tightest bound</h3>

$$
\begin{aligned}\max_{\beta_0,\,\beta\in B}\quad &\beta_0+\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n\mathbb E_\nu[\varphi_n(s)]\\\mathrm{s.t.}\quad &\beta_0\le\min_{(s,a)\in D}f(\beta;s,a).\end{aligned}
$$

</div>
<div class="equation-box saddle-stage fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="1">
<h3>Eliminate the intercept and define F</h3>

$$
F=\max_{\beta\in B}\left\{\min_{(s,a)\in D}f(\beta;s,a)+\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n\mathbb E_\nu[\varphi_n(s)]\right\}.
$$

$$
\beta_0^*=\min_{(s,a)\in D}f(\beta;s,a).
$$

</div>
<div class="equation-box saddle-stage fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="2">
<h3>Lift the minimum to a search over densities</h3>

$$
\min_{(s,a)\in D}f(\beta;s,a)=\inf_{y\in Y}\mathbb E_y[f(\beta;s,a)].
$$

$$
F=\max_{\beta\in B}\inf_{y\in Y}\left\{\mathbb E_y[f(\beta;s,a)]+\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n\mathbb E_\nu[\varphi_n(s)]\right\}.
$$

</div>
<div class="equation-box saddle-stage fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="3">
<h3>Regularize the density</h3>

$$
\mathbb E_y[f(\beta;s,a)]\;\longrightarrow\;\mathbb E_y[f(\beta;s,a)]+\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y\Vert p_u).
$$

$$
\lambda>0,\qquad p_u\text{ is the uniform density on }D.
$$

</div>
<div class="equation-box saddle-stage fragment current-visible" data-fragment-index="4">
<h3>The regularized saddle point problem</h3>

$$
F(\lambda)=\max_{\beta\in B}\min_{y\in Y}\left\{\mathbb E_y[f(\beta;s,a)]+\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(y\Vert p_u)+\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n\mathbb E_\nu[\varphi_n(s)]\right\}.
$$

</div>
<div class="equation-box saddle-stage density-stage fragment" data-fragment-index="5">
<h3>Three ways to find restrictive constraints</h3>
```{=html}
<div class="constraint-density-demo">
<span class="fragment density-generation-step" data-fragment-index="6" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<span class="fragment density-learning-step" data-fragment-index="7" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<div class="density-methods" role="group" aria-label="Highlight a constraint method"><button type="button" data-density-mode="uniform" aria-pressed="true">Constraint sampling <small>Uniform over the domain</small></button><button type="button" data-density-mode="minimum">Constraint generation <small>Find the minimum of f</small></button><button type="button" data-density-mode="learned" aria-pressed="false">Constraint violation learning <small>Learn where low values occur</small></button></div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 1100 250" class="constraint-density-svg" role="img" aria-label="Illustrative constraint threshold curve with a global minimum, a uniform density, and a learned density concentrated near low values."><path d="M45 18V210H1070" fill="none" stroke="#8ba1ac"/><path data-density-uniform fill="#397e9133" stroke="#397e91"/><path data-density-learned fill="#d77b7355" stroke="#d77b73" stroke-width="2"/><path data-density-curve fill="none" stroke="#192c7b" stroke-width="4"/><circle data-density-min r="7" fill="#ad3c35"/><text data-density-min-label fill="#ad3c35" font-size="18">min f</text><text x="62" y="35" fill="#192c7b" font-size="18">Constraint threshold f over state-action pairs</text><text x="550" y="242" text-anchor="middle" font-size="18">State-action pairs (s, a) · illustrative domain</text></svg>
<div class="density-slider"><label for="constraint-density-lambda">Regularization strength</label><input id="constraint-density-lambda" type="range" min="0" max="100" value="35" aria-label="Regularization strength, from concentrated to nearly uniform"><span data-density-value></span></div>
<p class="density-explanation" data-density-explanation></p>
</div>
```
</div>

</div>

:::

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Define the domain D and density set Y before using either. Step one eliminates the intercept because the ALP objective increases in beta-zero. Step two lifts the nonconvex point search to a linear expectation over densities without changing its value. Step three adds KL regularization relative to the uniform density. This is the construct step of CVL: it builds a sampleable alternative to repeatedly solving the global separation problem.
:::

## The optimal density is Gibbs {#s32 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide .gibbs-combined-slide}

::: {.slide-body}
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
<p class="muted">For fixed $\beta\in B$ and $\lambda>0$</p>

$$
y^*_{\lambda,\beta}(s,a)=
\frac{\exp[-f(\beta;s,a)/\lambda]}
{\displaystyle\int_D\exp[-f(\beta;s',a')/\lambda]\,d(s',a')}.
$$

::: {.compact-list}
- Smaller $\lambda$ sharpens mass around minimizers of $f$.
- Metropolis–Hastings can sample using the unnormalized numerator $\exp[-f(\beta;s,a)/\lambda]$.
:::

<p class="story-line"><strong>The construct step now has a closed-form target density that can be sampled.</strong></p>
:::
::: {.column width="55%" .fragment data-fragment-index="0"}
<h3>From concentrated to more diffuse</h3>

```{=html}

lambdas = (10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000)
plot_gibbs_simulation(beta_1, beta_2, lambdas)</textarea>
 <div class="demo-controls">

 </div>

</div>
```

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
For fixed coefficients and positive lambda the optimal sampling distribution is the normalized Gibbs density. Metropolis–Hastings uses ratios of the unnormalized numerator, so the normalizing integral is not required. Reveal the runnable browser Python comparison on the right. Its three panels use the same coefficients and increase lambda from 10 through 100 to 1000. Small lambda concentrates near low constraint thresholds; increasing lambda spreads probability more broadly. Edit the sequence to explore further; this computes densities on a grid rather than drawing an MCMC trajectory. The open circle identifies the grid minimizer of f, and the star identifies the independently computed grid mode of the Gibbs density. They coincide for fixed coefficients at every positive lambda.
:::

## Primal-dual updates in PSMD algorithm {#s35 .content-slide .continuous-import-slide}

::: {.slide-body}
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="51%"}
<div class="psmd-update-row">
<h3>1 · Initialize and sample</h3>

- Initialize coefficients to zero and the sampling distribution to uniform; draw a state–action pair.

$$\beta^{(0)}=0,\quad y^{(0)}=p_u,\qquad(\widehat s_t,\widehat a_t)\sim y^{(t)}.$$

</div>
<div class="psmd-update-row fragment" data-fragment-index="0">
<h3>2 · Estimate the gradient and update coefficients</h3>

$$
\widehat L_t(\beta)=\frac{c(\widehat s_t,\widehat a_t)-\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n[\varphi_n(\widehat s_t)-\gamma\varphi_n(\check s_t)]}{1-\gamma}
+\sum_{n=1}^N\beta_n\mathbb E_\nu[\varphi_n(S)].
$$

$$\widehat g_t=\nabla_\beta\widehat L_t(\beta^{(t)}),\qquad
\beta^{(t+1)}=\Pi_B(\beta^{(t)}+\eta_t\widehat g_t).$$

<p class="tiny muted">Next-state sample: $\check s_t\sim P(\cdot\mid\widehat s_t,\widehat a_t)$.</p>
</div>
<div class="psmd-update-row fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
<h3>3 · KL mirror descent for $y$</h3>

$$
y^{(t+1)}(s,a)\propto[y^{(t)}(s,a)]^{\frac{1}{1+\eta_t\lambda_t}}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{\eta_t\widehat f_t(\beta^{(t)};s,a)}{1+\eta_t\lambda_t}\right].
$$

</div>
:::
::: {.column width="49%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
```{=html}
<div class="continuous-python-lab" data-continuous-python data-demo-id="psmd-samples" data-demo-autorun="false">
 <label class="demo-editor-label" for="demo-psmd-samples">Run Python, then move through the sampled constraints</label>
 <textarea id="demo-psmd-samples" data-demo-editor rows="5" spellcheck="false" aria-label="Editable Python for PSMD samples focus over time">iterations = 180
temperature = 35.0
seed = 777
psmd_demo = run_psmd_demo(iterations, temperature, seed)
plot_psmd_sample_sequence(psmd_demo)</textarea>
 <div class="demo-controls">
  <button type="button" data-demo-run>Run Python</button>
  <button type="button" data-demo-stop disabled>Stop</button>
  <button type="button" data-demo-reset>Reset</button>
  <span data-demo-status role="status">Ready · runs in your browser</span>
 </div>
 <div class="demo-output" data-demo-output aria-live="polite"><p class="demo-hint">Run Python to generate the plot.</p></div>
</div>
```


:::
:::
:::

{{< include /components/logos.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Initialize coefficients at zero and a uniform density, then sample state-action pairs from the current density. A next-state sample gives the stochastic gradient estimate. Projected ascent updates the coefficients immediately after gradient estimation; the KL mirror step updates the density. The right panel is a lightweight teaching implementation with persistent Metropolis particles and fixed sampling temperature, rather than an exact numerical reproduction of the displayed decreasing-regularization mirror update. It preserves the run for the following bounds slide. Each frame shows one iteration snapshot, with sampled state and action on the axes, not a density heatmap. Run Python and use Previous and Next to inspect the six snapshots.
:::
